nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a type of alternatives containing three distinct elements, and let $E$ be a finite nonempty set of voters. A profile $P$ assigns to every voter $v$ a relation $P_v$ on $A$; it is admissible if, for every $v \in E$, $P_v$ is a total preorder (reflexive, transitive, and $P_v(x, y)$ or $P_v(y, x)$ for all $x, y \in A$). For a relation $R$ on $A$, say $R$ strictly ranks $a$ above $b$ if $R(a, b)$ holds and…
nodes.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem for weak preferences

nodes.summary: Suppose there are finitely many alternatives, at least three of them, and finitely many voters, at least one. Then every social welfare function, which assigns a strict total order of the alternatives to each profile of strict total orders (one per voter), that satisfies the Pareto condition and independence of irrelevant alternatives is dictatorial.
nodes.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem for strict preferences, general form

nodes.summary: Suppose there are finitely many alternatives, at least three of them, and finitely many voters, at least one. Then every social welfare function, which assigns a strict total order of the alternatives to each profile of strict total orders (one per voter), that satisfies the Pareto condition and independence of irrelevant alternatives is dictatorial.
nodes.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem for strict preferences

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a strict total order on a type $\alpha$, and write $a \lt _T b$ for its relation. Then for every $a \in \alpha$, $a \lt _T a$ does not hold.
nodes.title: Irreflexivity of strict preference (Arrow's theorem)

nodes.summary: A voter $d$ is a dictator for a social welfare function $F$ if for every profile $p$ and all alternatives $a, b$, whenever $d$ strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p$, the social order $F(p)$ also strictly prefers $a$ to $b$.
nodes.title: Dictator of a social welfare function

nodes.summary: A social welfare function $F$ is dictatorial if some voter $d$ is a dictator for $F$: for every profile $p$ and all alternatives $a, b$, whenever $d$ strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p$, the social order $F(p)$ also strictly prefers $a$ to $b$.
nodes.title: Dictatorial social welfare function

nodes.summary: A social welfare function $F$ satisfies independence of irrelevant alternatives if for all profiles $p_1, p_2$ and all alternatives $a, b$ the following holds: if every voter strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p_1$ exactly when that voter strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p_2$, then $F(p_1)$ strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ exactly when $F(p_2)$ does.
nodes.title: Independence of irrelevant alternatives

nodes.summary: A social welfare function $F$ satisfies the Pareto condition if for every profile $p$ and all alternatives $a, b$, whenever every voter strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p$, the social order $F(p)$ also strictly prefers $a$ to $b$.
nodes.title: Pareto condition

nodes.summary: For a strict total order $T$ on a type $\alpha$, this is its underlying binary relation $\lt _T$ on $\alpha$.
nodes.title: Preference relation of a strict total order (Arrow's theorem)

nodes.summary: A relation $<$ on a type $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$) defines a strict total order on $\alpha$.
nodes.title: Strict total order from a relation (Arrow's theorem)

nodes.summary: A profile assigns to each voter a strict total order on the alternatives.
nodes.title: Preference profile (Arrow's theorem)

nodes.summary: A social welfare function maps each unrestricted profile to a social strict total order.
nodes.title: Social welfare function

nodes.summary: A strict total order on a type $\alpha$ consists of a relation $<$ on $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$). Here it models a strict preference over alternatives.
nodes.title: Strict preference orders for Arrow's theorem

nodes.summary: If $<$ is a strict total order on a type $\alpha$ and $a, b \in \alpha$ are distinct, then $a < b$ or $b < a$.
nodes.title: Strict preference orders for Arrow's theorem are total

nodes.summary: If $<$ is a strict total order on a type $\alpha$ and $a, b, c \in \alpha$ satisfy $a < b$ and $b < c$, then $a < c$.
nodes.title: Strict preference orders for Arrow's theorem are transitive

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
